title: Bigger Bodies, Less Surface per Volume

scenes.tts: A thirty gram mouse and a seventy kilogram human. The human is more than two thousand times heavier. Yet a widely used fit for mammals predicts it burns only about three hundred and forty times the energy. Each kilogram of mouse burns about seven times more than each kilogram of human. Why?
scenes.visual: Two animal labels; a mass bar about 2,300 times longer, an energy bar about 340 times; a question mark on the per kilogram gap.
scenes.narration: A thirty gram mouse and a seventy kilogram human. The human is more than two thousand times heavier. scenes.tts: Everything a body exchanges crosses its surface. Model a cell as an ideal cube. Double its side, and the area grows four times, but the volume grows eight times. So the surface area to volume ratio halves, from zero point six to zero point three per micrometre. These cubes are illustrative, not measured cells.

scenes.tts: Diffusion is the net spread of molecules from crowded places to less crowded ones. In a simple model, the typical time is the distance squared, divided by two times the diffusion coefficient. For a small solute in water, ten micrometres takes about zero point zero five seconds. One centimetre takes about fourteen hours.

scenes.tts: Animals and plants meet the same geometry with the same four answers. Flattening keeps every cell near the outside, in a planarian flatworm and a leaf blade. Folding packs surface into a small space, in the alveoli of the mammalian lung and inside a leaf. Branching divides the airways again and again, and splits leaf veins into finer veins. Bulk flow moves a whole fluid, and diffusion still covers the last few micrometres.
scenes.visual: Four schematic panels build in turn: thin slab with arrows on both faces; folded bar; branching bars; a tube with a flow arrow ending in short diffusion arrows.

scenes.tts: A widely quoted fit for mammals says basal rate is seventy times mass to the power zero point seven five, in kilocalories a day. That gives a thirty gram mouse about five kilocalories a day, and a seventy kilogram adult human about one thousand seven hundred. Per kilogram, that is about one hundred sixty eight for the mouse and twenty four for the human. The exponent is below one, so rate per kilogram falls as animals get bigger.
scenes.caption: A widely quoted fit for mammals says basal rate is 70 x M^0.75, in kcal a day. That gives a 30 g mouse about 5 kcal a day, and a 70 kg adult human about 1,700. Per kilogram, that is about 168 for the mouse and 24 for the human. The exponent is below 1, so rate per kilogram falls as animals get bigger.
scenes.visual: The fit as a formula; totals for mouse and human as chips; per kilogram bars 168 against 24.

scenes.tts: Treat three quarters as a fit, not a law. White and Seymour found a mammalian exponent near two thirds, once body temperature and digestive state were controlled. With two thirds, the mouse's advantage per kilogram becomes about thirteen times, not seven. The cause of the exponent is still debated. Keep this rule: in larger bodies surface falls behind volume, so flow carries material, and diffusion covers the last few micrometres.
scenes.caption: Treat 3/4 as a fit, not a law. White and Seymour found a mammalian exponent near 2/3, once body temperature and digestive state were controlled. Keep this rule: in larger bodies surface falls behind volume, so flow carries material, and diffusion covers the last few micrometres.
